description:
I'm an enthusiastic student from Peshawar, Pakistan, who loves exploring, learning, and sharing knowledge. I'm excited to participate in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and collaborate with creative, curious students.

I'm looking for teammates preferably (14-15 years girl) interested in space science, technology, design, and storytelling. No expertise required—just curiosity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn!

Learn more: https://alizahayat.online/
summary:
Digital Space Museum: The Stories We Left Behind
We built a free, multilingual Digital Space Museum for the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars." It features six machines humans left behind: the Apollo 11 descent stage, the Apollo 17 lunar rover, a lunar laser retroreflector, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter and Perseverance's landing debris. Each machine tells its own story, illustrated with authentic NASA photographs, and hands-on labs let students do real science, such as measuring the distance to the Moon with a laser.
Every story is available in six languages: English, Urdu, Pashto, Arabic, French and Spanish, with careful right-to-left typography for Urdu, Pashto and Arabic. Student narrator Aliza Hayat recorded the English, Urdu and Pashto stories, and our Your Voice, Your Story invitation asks young volunteers to record the rest.
The museum opens on an ordinary phone, as a website or a small Android app, with no account and no cost. It is built by young people, for young people, so that no child is left out of space because of language.
details:
• The Digital Space Museum is a free website and Android app about six machines humans left on the Moon and Mars: the Apollo 11 descent stage, the Apollo 17 lunar rover, a laser retroreflector, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter and Perseverance's landing debris. Each machine tells its own story ("I am Ingenuity") scene by scene, with authentic NASA photographs. Every exhibit ends with a photo gallery, a quiz question and cited science facts.
  • The museum works in six languages: English, Urdu, Pashto, Arabic, French and Spanish. Student narrator Aliza Hayat recorded the English, Urdu and Pashto stories. For Arabic, French and Spanish, the visitor's device reads the story in that language, never in an English voice. A Share Your Voice form invites young volunteers to record more, with guardian consent for under-18s.
Benefits
  • Children learn space science in their home language, including three right-to-left languages that space resources rarely cover.
  • It runs on an ordinary phone, with no account and no cost. The Android app (2.4 MB) installs straight from the website and updates itself.
  • It's ready for classrooms: any exhibit can be shown fullscreen on a projector.

Intended impact

  • Every curious child, whatever language they speak, should feel that space belongs to them too. The museum connects young people to real missions through stories they remember, and invites them to take part as narrators, not just listeners.
Tools and technology
  • Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework, so it's light on slow connections
  • Audio: phone recordings (MP3) and the browser's Web Speech API
  • Fonts: Noto Nastaliq Urdu, Noto Naskh Arabic and Inter, bundled with the site
  • Android app: web app manifest, packaged with PWABuilder
  • Development: Node.js, Playwright browser tests at phone, tablet and desktop sizes, VS Code, Git, GitHub
  • Hosting: Vercel and GitHub Pages
  • Volunteer form: Google Forms
  • Content: NASA Image and Video Library, NASA/JPL mission pages and NASA YouTube clips
  • AI assistance: Claude Code helped write code, run tests and draft translations; ChatGPT generated the logo

How it is creative

  • Honest voices: a human narrator where we have one, a matching device voice where we don't, and an open invitation for young volunteers to share “Your Voice Your Story”.
  • Machines with a voice: a rover or a helicopter becomes a character children remember, not a list of facts.
  • A museum in your pocket: a collection, exhibits and a gallery, designed for a phone screen.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: authentic NASA photographs only, cited figures, simulations labelled as simulations, and unreviewed translations marked as drafts.
  • Language: separate text for each language, proper right-to-left layouts, and a suitable font for each script.
  • Accessibility: keyboard and screen-reader support, layouts tested down to 320-pixel-wide screens and with enlarged text, and nothing plays until the visitor presses Play.
  • Low bandwidth: a small site and app; videos load only when a visitor chooses to watch.
  • Children's safety: no tracking or analytics, and guardian consent before any child's recording is published.

Respect for NASA's guidelines: we follow NASA's media-use rules, use no NASA insignia and make no claim of NASA endorsement.
